tool_calls.result: 83.505 Electronic delivery of notices. — (1) A landlord or tenant may electronically deliver via an e-mail address any notices required under this part to the other party if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time. Such addendum must be in substantially the following form: Landlord election: Notices from a tenant may contain time-sensitive information about the tenant’s housing. The election to receive notices from the tenant by e-mail is voluntary. ☐ I (name) , the landlord or the landlord’s agent, agree to receive notices required by the rental agreement or under part II of chapter 83, Florida Statutes, from the tenant by e-mail. I designate the following e-mail address for receipt of notices from the tenant: (landlord’s or landlord’s agent’s e-mail address) . ☐ I do not agree to receive notices by e-mail. I may revoke my agreement to receive notices by e-mail by providing written notice to the tenant which is effective upon delivery of such written notice and does not affect the validity of any notice that was previously sent by e-mail. I may update my e-mail address designated for electronic delivery at any time by providing written notice to the tenant specifying the new e-mail address, which takes effect upon delivery of such notice. Tenant election: Notices from a landlord may contain time-sensitive information about a tenant’s housing. The election to receive notices from the landlord by e-mail is voluntary. ☐ I (name) , the tenant, agree to receive notices required by the rental agreement or under part II of chapter 83, Florida Statutes, from the landlord by e-mail. I designate the following e-mail address for receipt of notices from the landlord: (tenant’s e-mail address) . ☐ I do not agree to receive notices by e-mail. I may revoke my agreement to receive notices by e-mail by providing written notice to the landlord which is effective upon delivery of such written notice and does not affect the validity of any notice that was previously sent by e-mail. I may update my e-mail address designated for electronic delivery at any time by providing written notice to the landlord specifying the new e-mail address, which takes effect upon delivery of such notice. (2) A party who agrees to electronic delivery may revoke such agreement at any time by providing written notice to the other party. Such revocation takes effect upon delivery of the written notice to the other party and does not affect the validity of any notice previously sent by e-mail. (3) A party may update the e-mail address designated for electronic delivery at any time by providing written notice to the other party specifying the new e-mail address. The update takes effect upon delivery of the written notice to the other party. (4) A notice sent electronically pursuant to this section is deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable. (5) The sender of the e-mail must maintain a copy of any notice sent electronically and evidence of the transmission of the e-mail. (6) This section does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law. History. — s. 1, ch. 2025-16.

(c) If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney. The court shall advance the cause on the calendar.
7. NOTICES TO LANDLORD. Written notices to Landlord shall be delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail.

answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, it looks like you can get all $1,050 back. Your landlord had 30 days after your lease ended to send you a written notice that it was keeping part of the deposit, and the facts you confirmed show it sent none. That 30-day period ended on 2026-08-30, which has passed. A landlord that misses that deadline loses the right to deduct anything from the deposit. It can still sue you for damages, but only after it returns the deposit. One fact could change this answer, and I have to ask about it.

Your lease says you must be enrolled as a student, and that the landlord can end the lease if you aren't. The state's rental law doesn't cover housing that comes only as a side part of a school's services. Nothing in your lease says a school owns or runs the building. Is Lakeview Terrace run by or for Alachua Valley College, or could you live there only while you were enrolled?

DETAILS

### Does Florida's deposit law cover your apartment?
- **The enrollment clause leaves doubt.** The law does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)).
- **What the lease shows.** The landlord is Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, "as agent for the owner" (Lease §1). Clause 11 says you "must be enrolled as a student at Alachua Valley College" and that the landlord "may end this lease if Tenant is not enrolled."
- **Both readings are possible.** If this is an ordinary private apartment with an enrollment rule, the deposit law applies. If the housing is run by or for the college, the law may not apply. Your answer will tell us which.
- **No sign of government housing.** Neither the lease nor you mentioned public housing or a rent subsidy, so I am not treating that as an issue.

### Did your landlord lose the right to keep any of the deposit?
Three things must all be true. On your confirmed facts, all three are met.
1. **No proper notice came.** The landlord had to send written notice of a claim "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.49(3)(a)). You confirmed you received nothing, by any means. Your lease also says the parties did not agree to e-mail notices (Lease §8).
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Your lease ended 2026-07-31, and 30 days after that was 2026-08-30. The 15-day deadline for returning a deposit when the landlord claims nothing was 2026-08-15. Both have passed. You moved out on the same day the lease ended, so the move-out date gives the same result.
3. **You did not need to give notice before leaving.** That duty applies to tenants who leave before the lease ends or who rent week to week or month to month (83.49(5)). You stayed until the lease ended on a fixed term. You also mailed your forwarding address in writing on 2026-07-28.

The statute's words are: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)).

In plain terms, the whole $1,050 is owed to you. Your landlord could still sue you for damages afterward, but it can't subtract them from the deposit.

### What if the landlord still doesn't pay?
Either side may sue to settle who gets the deposit. In that case, "the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). That applies only to whoever wins, so you could also be ordered to pay if you lose. The same paragraph says the court hears these cases sooner: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar."

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. The $350 fee isn't treated as a security deposit, so the landlord doesn't have to return it the way it would a deposit. Florida's law says a fee paid instead of a deposit "is not a security deposit." Your lease and your signed fee agreement also both call the fee nonrefundable. The landlord did miss a notice deadline, but the law doesn't say that makes the landlord give the fee back. Whether your fee agreement follows the law's required terms is something you can check, and it could matter.

Can you look at the fee agreement you signed on July 10, 2025? Does it say that you could end the fee arrangement at any time and pay a regular security deposit instead? Does it also include a boxed notice that begins "FEE IN LIEU OF SECURITY DEPOSIT"?

DETAILS

### Is the $350 fee a "security deposit" under Florida law?
- No. Section 83.491(6) says a fee collected in lieu of a deposit "is not a security deposit as defined in s. 83.43 (13)."
- The deposit-return rules, including the loss of the landlord's claim for missing the notice deadline, are in section 83.49(3)(a). They apply to security deposits.
- So the usual deposit rule doesn't apply here. That rule says a landlord who misses the 30-day notice loses its claim on the deposit and must return all of it.
- Your lease (¶5) says: "Landlord holds no security deposit for this lease." You also confirmed that you paid no deposit.
- Nothing in the lease ties your housing to a school. Section 83.42(1) is therefore not a concern, and part II applies.

### Can the landlord keep a "nonrefundable" fee?
- Section 83.491(3)(f) lets the landlord tell the tenant "That the fee is nonrefundable, if applicable."
- Your lease (¶5) says: "The fee is nonrefundable." You told me the fee agreement says the same.
- The statute gives no right to a refund of a fee like this.
- This does not mean the landlord can keep money for other things. The fee only secures occupancy without a deposit.

### What did the landlord have to do, and did it?
- Section 83.491(2)(a) says the landlord "must notify the tenant within 30 days after the conclusion of the tenancy if there are any costs or fees due." Examples are unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear.
- Your lease ended July 31, 2026, and that is also the day you moved out. Thirty days from then ended on 2026-08-30, which has passed. You say you received no notice by any means, so the landlord missed this deadline.
- Section 83.491 does not say what happens when the landlord misses this deadline. It has no loss-of-claim sentence like the one in section 83.49(3)(a).
- It is not settled whether the missed notice stops the landlord from later charging you for costs. One reading is that no consequence is written, so the landlord keeps its claims. The other is that the notice would have no purpose unless missing it limited the landlord. The statute doesn't choose.
- This does not give you a right to the $350. It matters if the landlord later tries to bill you for damage or unpaid amounts.

### Could the fee agreement itself change the answer?
- Section 83.491(4)(a) requires a signed written agreement. It must say that the agreement can be ended at any time if you pay the security deposit. It must also describe how the fee is collected and what happens if you default on paying it.
- Section 83.491(4)(b) requires a boxed disclosure "in substantially the following form," beginning "FEE IN LIEU OF SECURITY DEPOSIT."
- Section 83.491(3) also requires the landlord to tell you in writing about your options. For example, you could pay a regular deposit instead, or pay it in installments.
- Section 83.491 does not say what happens if the landlord left these out. If the fee agreement lacks them, there may be an argument that the fee wasn't properly set up. Whether that makes it refundable is unsettled, and I can't tell you which way it goes.
- I haven't seen the fee agreement. I only know from you that it is signed and calls the fee nonrefundable.

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
**Short answer:** Whether your landlord has already lost the right to keep any of your deposit is not settled. It depends on when the landlord's 30 days to send a claim notice started. If those days started when you moved out, the deadline has passed and the landlord must return all $1,050. If they started when the lease ended, the landlord has until August 30 to send you a claim notice. You did what the law required before leaving early, and the landlord has sent you nothing. So if no proper notice arrives by the later deadline, you should get the whole deposit back. Even then, the landlord could still sue you for damages afterward.

DETAILS

### Does Florida's deposit law cover your rental?
Yes, as far as I can tell. Your lease is with a private management company, Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, acting as agent for the owner. Nothing in it ties the apartment to a school, and nothing in it points to public housing or a rent subsidy. The law excludes rent or deposits that are "regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)). If a government program pays part of your rent or sets it, tell me, because that could change the answer.

### Did you give the notice the law requires for leaving early?
Yes. You left before the lease ended on July 31, 2026. A tenant who does that "must give at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (83.49(5)).
- You sent a certified letter on June 1, and the office signed for it on June 3.
- The letter gave your move-out date and your new address.
- The last day to give 7 days' notice for a June 15 move-out was June 8. Your letter was sent and received before that.
- Your lease does not set a different rule. Section 7 says to deliver written notices to the office "by hand" or by "certified mail," which is what you did. Section 6 asks for a forwarding address in writing, and your letter gave one.

So the landlord is not excused from sending a claim notice. The landlord can't say you skipped a required step.

### Has the landlord lost the right to make a claim?
This is the open point. The landlord must give written notice of a claim "within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement." The notice must go "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address" or by e-mail under 83.505 (83.49(3)(a)). Your lease says the parties have not agreed to e-mail notices (section 8). The statute doesn't say which date ends the rental agreement when a tenant leaves early. There are two readings:
- **Move-out date (June 15):** The 30 days ended July 15, and that has passed. The statute's required disclosure to tenants says the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)). Under this reading, the landlord has forfeited any claim. The statute says the landlord "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant" (83.49(3)(a)). That means the full $1,050 comes back to you.
- **Lease end date (July 31):** The 30 days end August 30, and that has not passed. The statute begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). That wording treats vacating and termination as two separate things. Under this reading, the landlord can still send a proper claim notice until August 30. A certified-mail notice to the address you gave would be the kind the statute requires.

I can't tell you which reading a court would choose.

### What if the landlord sends a claim notice?
Say it arrives by certified mail at your new address within the time allowed. If you don't object in writing within 15 days after you receive it, the landlord may deduct the claim. The landlord must then send you the rest within 30 days after the date of the notice (83.49(3)(b)). Not objecting doesn't stop you from suing later (83.49(3)(b)). If you object in time, the statute sets no step after that except a court case. What happens next would be unsettled.

### Is the landlord late on the 15-day return?
Not yet, on the lease-end reading. If the landlord intends no claim, the deposit is due "within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). Counted from July 31, that is August 15, and it has not passed. Missing that date by itself would not cost the landlord its claim while the 30-day period is still running.

### What if this goes to court?
If either side sues over the deposit, the winner gets "court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." The court must also "advance the cause on the calendar," so these cases are heard sooner (83.49(3)(c)).

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, you can get the $250 back. Your friend is only partly right. Most of Florida's deposit law doesn't apply to a housing authority, but the part about returning a deposit does. On the facts you've confirmed, the authority's 30 days to claim any of your deposit ended on 2026-08-30. It sent no claim, so it lost the right to keep any of the money.

The authority can still sue you later for damages, but it has to return your deposit first. If you sue over the deposit and win, you can recover your court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

DETAILS

### Does Florida's deposit law cover public housing?
Partly. Section 83.49(4) says the section does not apply to housing authorities created under chapter 421, "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6)". Your lease (¶1) says Riverbend Housing Authority is a public housing agency created under chapter 421, so those three subsections apply to you.

Subsection (3) is the rule on returning deposits and on claims against them. The parts that don't apply to the authority are the rules on how it holds the deposit and on interest. Your lease (¶5) says no interest is owed, and that doesn't affect your right to the deposit.

Your lease is an ordinary residential lease. Nothing in it ties your housing to a school or to services, so the exclusions in 83.42(1) don't appear to apply.

### Did the authority lose its right to keep any of the deposit?
Based on what you've confirmed, yes. Three things must all be true:

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached you.** Section 83.49(3)(a) requires a written notice "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address" or by e-mail under a signed addendum. You confirmed you got no notice by any means. Your lease (¶8) also says no e-mail agreement exists.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Your lease ended 2026-07-31. Thirty days from then is 2026-08-30, and that date has passed. Under 83.49(3)(a), "within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement" is the deadline for the claim notice.
3. **The authority wasn't excused from giving notice.** Section 83.49(5) excuses the notice only for a tenant who leaves before the lease ends or who has a periodic tenancy (week to week, month to month and so on). You stayed until the lease ended on 2026-07-31, and nothing in your lease or your account shows a periodic tenancy. So the notice duty applied to the authority.

Section 83.49(3)(a) then says that if the landlord fails to give the notice in time, it "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." Forfeits means loses the right. So the whole $250 is owed to you. The authority could still sue you for damages afterward.

The authority also had to return the deposit within 15 days if it planned no claim. That date was 2026-08-15, and it has passed.

### What if the authority sends a notice now?
A late notice shouldn't revive its claim. The 30-day window under 83.49(3)(a) closed on 2026-08-30.

### Can you recover court costs?
Section 83.49(3)(c) says that if either side sues over the deposit, "the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." That applies only to the winner. The same paragraph says the court hears these cases sooner.

### Does your forwarding address matter?
Your lease (¶6) required a written forwarding address, and you mailed one on 2026-07-28. The authority's silence doesn't depend on it. Because no notice came at all, the forfeiture applies either way.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
**No, not automatically.** The rule that makes a landlord give back the whole deposit for missing the 30-day notice deadline probably doesn't help you here. For a month-to-month tenant, that rule depends on written notice before leaving, and you gave only spoken notice. You still have a right to your deposit, and the landlord has not returned it. Whether the landlord can keep any of it is not decided by the missing notice.

Does the landlord have a real reason to keep part of it, such as unpaid rent or damage to the apartment? Has anyone from the landlord's side mentioned one?

DETAILS

### Did the landlord miss the deadline?
- Your move-out date was Aug 31, 2026. The 30-day deadline for a claim notice was Sept 30, 2026, and it has passed. The 15-day return date was Sept 15, 2026, and it has also passed.
- The landlord sent no notice of a claim, and you gave a written forwarding address on Aug 31.
- Under 83.49(3)(a), a landlord who intends a claim must send written notice by certified mail within 30 days. A landlord who misses that deadline "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit."

### Why the forfeiture rule probably doesn't apply to you
- You rent month to month, so 83.49(5) applies to you. A month-to-month tenant "must give at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating," and the notice must include an address where the tenant can be reached.
- Your lease has no different rule. Clause 7 only says written notices go by hand to the office or by certified mail.
- You told the manager in person on July 20 and put nothing in writing. The last day for a written notice would have been Aug 24, 2026.
- 83.49(5) then says: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it."
- Your landlord's silence therefore forfeits nothing. Your oral notice does not cost you the deposit either.

### Is the deposit still yours?
- Yes. The deposit is $1,050 under lease clause 5.
- The law says only that you keep "any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." It does not say what the landlord may keep when it never sent a notice.
- The result depends on whether the landlord has a real claim, such as unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear. That is why I asked.
- If the landlord has no claim, 83.49(3)(a) requires it to return the deposit within 15 days after the rental ended. That date has passed.

### What if this goes to court?
- 83.49(3)(c) covers a lawsuit over the deposit. "The prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." The winner gets this, whichever side that is.
- The same paragraph says the court "shall advance the cause on the calendar," so these cases are heard sooner.
- Even if the landlord had a claim, your missing the written notice would not cost you the right to get back whatever part of the deposit it can't justify keeping.
