# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
Not settled. The 30-day deadline you remember was 30 days from the date of the landlord's letter, which was Sept. 19, and that date has passed. But the sentence that sets that deadline begins "Unless the tenant objects," and you did object. The statute doesn't say what the landlord must do after an objection, so I can't say the $650 is overdue. I also can't say it isn't. The only step the statute names is a court case.

The landlord did not lose its claim. Its letter was on time and sent the right way, so you don't get the whole $1,050 back on that ground. Your objection was also on time. The only route the statute sets out is going to court, and the winner can recover court costs and attorney fees.

DETAILS

### Did the landlord give the notice of its claim on time and the right way?
Yes, on the facts you confirmed. The law says that to claim part of the deposit, the landlord must send "written notice by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address" within 30 days after the rental agreement ends (83.49(3)(a)). Your lease ended July 31, 2026, so the 30 days ended Aug. 30, 2026. The landlord's letter is dated Aug. 20, 2026. It went by certified mail to the forwarding address you gave in writing. It named the amount ($400), the reason (carpet replacement), the 15-day objection window, and where to send an objection. So the landlord has not forfeited its claim, which would have meant losing the right to keep any of the deposit (83.49(3)(a)). Your lease is a normal apartment lease. Nothing in it ties your housing to a school, so I treated the deposit law as applying.

### Did you object in time?
Yes. You had 15 days from receiving the notice (83.49(3)(b)). You received it Aug. 24, so your last day was Sept. 8, 2026. You sent your objection Aug. 30, and the office signed for it Sept. 1. Both dates are before Sept. 8.

### Was the landlord required to send the $650 by now?
This is not settled. The statute says: "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord's claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord's notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)). The 30 days from the Aug. 20 letter ended Sept. 19, 2026. There are two readings:
- **First reading:** The right to deduct and the duty to send the balance both belong to the case where the tenant does not object. Because you objected, the text sets no deadline for the $650.
- **Second reading:** The 30 days is the only deadline the statute gives for returning the balance. Your objection challenged only the $400, so the $650 should have gone out by Sept. 19.

I'm not choosing between them.

### What can you do now?
After an objection, the statute names only one step, which is a court case. "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party's right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). Only the winner gets costs and fees, and the loser may have to pay them. The same paragraph says "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar," so these cases are heard sooner. The statute's notice to tenants also says you "should attempt to informally resolve any dispute before filing a lawsuit" (83.49(2)(d)).

Your lease has no clause that changes any of this. Section 6 covers move-out and your forwarding address. Section 7 covers how you send notices to the landlord. Neither addresses what happens after you object.

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
**Yes, you can ask for all $1,050 back, and the law supports you.** The landlord's letter gave no reason for keeping the $400. The law requires a notice of a claim to state the reason. The 30-day deadline for a proper notice has passed, so the landlord has lost the right to keep any of the deposit. Not objecting in writing doesn't change that. The landlord can still sue you for actual damages, but only after it returns the deposit.

My one question is whether the landlord sent you anything else in writing about the deposit before August 30, 2026. A second letter or a message giving a reason for the $400 would change my answer.

DETAILS

### Does Florida's deposit law cover you?
Yes, as far as I can tell. Your lease is a private apartment lease with Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC. Nothing in it ties the housing to a school, and nothing in it points to a government housing program. If your rent or deposit is set or paid by a program such as Section 8, tell me, because that could change things.

### Did the landlord give the required notice of a claim?
No. Under 83.49(3)(a), a landlord who intends to keep part of a deposit must send a written notice by certified mail within 30 days after the rental agreement ends. The notice must give "the intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim."
- The landlord used the right method. It sent the letter by certified mail to the forwarding address you gave in writing. Your lease at §8 also says notices go to that address after move-out.
- The letter you describe gave no reason for the $400. That leaves out something the statute requires.

### Has the 30-day deadline passed?
Yes. Your lease ended July 31, 2026. The 30 days ran out on 2026-08-30, and that date has passed. The landlord had no later chance to fix the notice.

### Did you have to do something first?
No. Section 83.49(5) requires advance written notice only from a tenant who leaves before the lease ends or who has a periodic tenancy, such as month-to-month. You stayed until the lease ended on July 31, 2026 (lease §3), so this rule doesn't apply to you.

### What does the landlord lose, and what can it still do?
Section 83.49(3)(a) says that if the landlord fails to give the required notice in time, it "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." In plain terms, the whole $1,050 is owed to you. The landlord may still sue you for damages after it returns the money.

### Does it matter that you didn't object?
It doesn't help the landlord. Your 15 days to object ended on 2026-09-08. Section 83.49(3)(b) says that missing the deadline "does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." The objection deadline matters only when the landlord's notice was valid.

There is a second reason the landlord is behind. Suppose a court treated the letter as a valid notice anyway. The landlord would still have had to send you the $650 balance within 30 days of the letter's date. That deadline was 2026-09-19, and it has passed. You have received nothing.

### What if you have to go to court?
Under 83.49(3)(c), if either side sues over the deposit, "the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." The court must also hear the case sooner. Those costs and fees go only to the winner, so they are not guaranteed.

Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

tool_calls.result: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant. — (1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord’s agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. In addition to posting the surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest. A landlord, or the landlord’s agent, engaged in the renting of dwelling units in five or more counties, who holds deposit moneys or advance rent and who is otherwise subject to the provisions of this section, may, in lieu of posting a surety bond in each county, elect to post a surety bond in the form and manner provided in this paragraph with the office of the Secretary of State. The bond shall be in the total amount of the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of tenants or in the amount of $250,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of this section. In addition to posting a surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest on the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of that tenant at the rate of 5 percent per year simple interest. (2) The landlord shall, in the lease agreement or within 30 days after receipt of advance rent or a security deposit, give written notice to the tenant which includes disclosure of the advance rent or security deposit. Subsequent to providing such written notice, if the landlord changes the manner or location in which he or she is holding the advance rent or security deposit, he or she must notify the tenant within 30 days after the change as provided in paragraphs (a)-(d). The landlord is not required to give new or additional notice solely because the depository has merged with another financial institution, changed its name, or transferred ownership to a different financial institution. This subsection does not apply to any landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units. Failure to give this notice is not a defense to the payment of rent when due. The written notice must: (a) Be given in person or delivered by mail or e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 to the tenant. (b) State the name and address of the depository where the advance rent or security deposit is being held or state that the landlord has posted a surety bond as provided by law. (c) State whether the tenant is entitled to interest on the deposit. (d) Contain the following disclosure: YOUR RENTAL AGREEMENT REQUIRES PAYMENT OF CERTAIN DEPOSITS. THE LANDLORD MAY TRANSFER ADVANCE RENTS TO THE LANDLORD’S ACCOUNT AS THEY ARE DUE AND WITHOUT NOTICE. answer:
Whether a letter with no dollar amount counts is not settled, and I can't say either way. The letter has some of what Florida requires. It came by certified mail, to the forwarding address you gave, and it states a reason (the carpet). It leaves out the amount. Either way, I'd send a written objection to the landlord's office before September 8, 2026, because that date has not passed.

- **If the letter counts:** your landlord can keep its claim, but only if you don't object in time. The landlord then has until September 19, 2026 to send you the rest of the deposit.
- **If the letter doesn't count:** your landlord loses the right to keep any of the deposit, and you are owed all $1,050. Your landlord could still sue you for the carpet afterward.
- **Why object now:** you don't have to decide which reading is right to protect yourself. An objection that says you dispute the claim and the amount keeps your position open under both readings.

DETAILS

### Is a notice with no amount the notice the law requires?
Section 83.49(3)(a) requires a landlord who wants to keep part of a deposit to give written notice "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address" of "his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." Your letter meets those parts. It was sent by certified mail to the forwarding address you gave, and it gives a reason.

The statute then says the notice "must contain a statement in substantially the following form." That form includes "in the amount of" a dollar figure. It also includes the 15-day warning to object and the address to send the objection to. Your letter has the warning and the address. It lacks the amount.

There are two readings, and the statute doesn't settle between them:
- **Reading one:** a notice without the amount is not the required notice. Under 83.49(3)(a), the landlord then "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant."
- **Reading two:** the form only has to be followed "substantially," so a letter with the reason, the warning, and the address is still enough.

### Was the letter on time?
Your lease ended and you moved out on July 31, 2026. The 30-day window ended August 30, 2026, which has passed. The letter is dated August 20 and you signed for it August 24, so it was on time under either date.

### What are your deadlines if the letter counts?
- **Your objection:** under 83.49(3)(b), you have 15 days after you receive the notice. You received it August 24, so the last day is **September 8, 2026**. That has not passed yet.
- **If you don't object:** the landlord "may then deduct the amount of his or her claim." The landlord must send you the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice. That date is **September 19, 2026**.
- **If you do object:** the statute sets no further step after an objection except a court case. I can't say whether the landlord may deduct, or when the balance would be due.
- **If you miss the deadline:** under 83.49(3)(b), a late objection "does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action."

### How should you send the objection?
Section 83.49(3)(b) lets you object to "the landlord's claim or the amount thereof." Your letter gave no amount, so you can object to both.

The statute only says the objection must be in writing. Your landlord's letter says to send it to the office address. Your lease (section 7) says written notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or sent there "by certified mail." Use one of those two ways, and keep a copy and your proof of delivery.

### What if this goes to court?
Under 83.49(3)(c), if either of you sues over the deposit, the winner "is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." The court must also hear the case sooner than usual.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.

Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.

Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
Your reading of the 30-day rule is partly right, but the statute doesn't clearly say what happens to the $650 after you object. It is not settled whether your landlord must still send the $650 while the $400 is disputed. The statute's 30-day deadline for sending the balance ran out on September 19. But the rule setting that deadline begins "Unless the tenant objects," and it says nothing about what the landlord must do once a tenant does object. Your landlord did send a proper claim notice, so you are not entitled to the whole $1,050 on the ground of a missing notice. The statute's only listed next step is a court case, where the winner can recover court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

DETAILS

### Did the landlord lose the right to claim the $400 by missing a deadline?

No, not on the facts you've confirmed. The landlord must send a written claim notice within 30 days after the lease ends. It must go by certified mail to your last known mailing address, and it must give the reason for the claim (83.49(3)(a)). If the landlord misses that, it "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit" (83.49(3)(a)). That would mean the whole deposit comes back to you, and the landlord could still sue you for damages afterward.

Here, the lease ended July 31, 2026, so the 30 days ran through August 30. Your landlord's letter is dated August 20 and went by certified mail to the forwarding address you gave in writing. It states the reason (carpet replacement) and the amount ($400). It also tells you to object within 15 days and says where to send the objection. That is the kind of notice the statute asks for. Your lease doesn't change this. It says notices go to your forwarding address after you move out (lease §8).

Also, you left on the lease's end date, so the early-departure notice rule in 83.49(5) doesn't come into play.

### Was your objection on time?

Your last day to object was September 8, 2026, which is 15 days after you received the notice on August 24 (83.49(3)(b)). You sent your written objection on August 30, and the office signed for it on September 1. You sent it to the address in the landlord's notice, as the lease requires (lease §7). So your objection was in writing and made within the 15 days.

### Was the $650 due within 30 days?

The statute says that unless the tenant objects, the landlord may deduct its claim and "shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim" (83.49(3)(b)). Counting from the August 20 notice date, that was September 19, and it has passed.

The deadline sits in the same sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects." The statute sets no step for what happens after a tenant objects. I can't say the $650 is overdue under the statute. I also can't say the landlord may keep holding it while the $400 is disputed. The text doesn't answer that.

### What happens now?

The statute's only listed route is a court case about the deposit. "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party's right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). Fees go only to the winning side, so a loss could cost you too. The same paragraph says "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar," which means the court hears these cases sooner.

Your objection also keeps your rights intact. The statute says a tenant's failure to object on time "does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action" (83.49(3)(b)). You objected on time, so your position is stronger than that.

Whether the carpet charge is fair is a question for a court. You say the wear is normal use, and the landlord says the carpet needs replacing. Nothing in the statute settles that.
